bibliography.abstract: We apply higher-order information measures to urban growth across borders and spatial units. We analyse 8,808 functional urban areas using gridded GDP estimates allocated from national accounts. Negative estimated O-information occurs in 29.93% of cross-border triplets and 2.00% of domestic triplets. This fifteen-fold contrast falls to fourfold at comparable dependence strength and persists under data-quality restrictions. Target-specific decompositions show how information overlaps or combines across cities. Administrative subdivisions have mean O-information within matched random-map ranges inside countries. These findings show why interpreting geographic dependence requires specifying comparison cities and spatial units, while economic connections remain to be established independently.
bibliography.title: Beyond city pairs: Higher-order information in urban growth across borders

en.caveats: The reliance on gridded GDP estimates derived from national accounts rather than direct local economic measurements requires establishing actual economic connections independently.
en.what: An analysis of cross-border and domestic urban growth across 8,808 functional urban areas using higher-order information measures and gridded national accounts GDP data reveals that negative O-information appears in 29.93% of cross-border triplets compared to 2.00% of domestic triplets. This fifteen-fold disparity decreases to fourfold when controlling for dependence strength, and target-specific decompositions demonstrate how growth information combines across regions. Furthermore, administrative subdivisions yield mean O-information within expected ranges for randomized spatial maps.
en.why: Researchers can no longer evaluate inter-urban spatial dependence using simple pairwise models, as higher-order interaction structures change fundamentally when crossing national boundaries versus internal administrative divisions.
